subtopic_detail: distinguishing a post enteric inflammatory arthritis from septic arthritis when the synovial white cell count is raised
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 27 year old man in the emergency department. Three weeks ago he had five days of profuse watery diarrhoea after a camping trip with friends, which settled without treatment. For the past five days his right knee has been swollen and painful and his left ankle has become sore, and this morning he could not put his heel to the ground.

He also describes both eyes being red and gritty for a week and pain where the back of his heel meets the bone. He injects no drugs, has no skin breaks and no indwelling lines. You aspirate the knee at the bedside and send the fluid urgently. The aspirate results return while he is still in the department.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, blood pressure 124/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right knee effusion with full but painful flexion, left ankle swollen, tenderness at the Achilles insertion, bilateral conjunctival injection
data_table.Investigations: Synovial fluid white cells 18 x10^9/L, Gram stain shows no organisms, no crystals seen under polarised light, C reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: High dose oral naproxen with review of the joints in two weeks
options.rationale: An asymmetrical lower limb oligoarthritis with enthesitis and conjunctivitis following a dysenteric illness is treated first with a full dose non steroidal anti inflammatory drug, which controls symptoms in most patients while the self limiting course runs. Culture negative fluid without crystals supports a reactive rather than infective process. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Arthroscopic washout with intravenous flucloxacillin for fourteen days
options.rationale: A synovial white cell count of 18 x10^9/L sits well below the range that usually accompanies pyogenic infection, and with no fever, a negative Gram stain and no portal of entry the pretest probability of a septic joint is low. This option would be correct if he were febrile with a synovial count above 50 x10^9/L or if the Gram stain were positive. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral doxycycline for three months to treat the triggering infection
options.rationale: Prolonged antibiotics have a possible role only where a genital chlamydial trigger is identified, and even then the evidence is contested. His trigger was enteric rather than urogenital, and antibiotics do not alter the course of the enteric form. (Source: Australian STI Management Guidelines)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily tapered over four weeks from today
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroid is reserved for polyarticular or refractory disease after a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug has been given an adequate trial. Starting it now commits him to a taper before the natural history has been observed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Weekly oral methotrexate with folic acid as initial disease control
options.rationale: A disease modifying agent is considered only when symptoms persist beyond about three to six months or the course becomes chronic and erosive. Reaching for it in the first week treats a condition that most often remits on its own. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

explanation.summary: An asymmetrical lower limb oligoarthritis appearing one to four weeks after an enteric or urogenital infection sits within the seronegative spondyloarthritis family, and enthesitis, dactylitis, conjunctivitis and mucocutaneous lesions are the extra articular clues that separate it from an isolated septic joint. Joint aspiration remains mandatory in any acute monoarthritis because the consequences of a missed infection are severe, but the fluid interpretation is what steers management rather than the decision to aspirate. Synovial counts above 50 x10^9/L with a neutrophil predominance point to infection, while counts in the 5 to 30 x10^9/L band with negative culture fit an inflammatory process. Most cases settle within three to six months, and HLA B27 positivity predicts a more protracted course rather than confirming the diagnosis. Persistent disease beyond six months warrants a disease modifying agent and rheumatology involvement.
key_points: Aspirate every acute monoarthritis, but read the count rather than assuming infection
Enthesitis at the Achilles insertion and conjunctivitis point away from a pyogenic joint
Full dose non steroidal anti inflammatory therapy is the first line treatment
Antibiotics do not shorten the post enteric form of the illness
Escalate to a disease modifying agent only if disease persists beyond three to six months
explanation.pearls: A synovial white cell count between 5 and 30 x10^9/L with a negative Gram stain and no crystals is the band where an inflammatory arthritis is far more likely than infection; above 50 x10^9/L treat as septic until culture proves otherwise.

subtopic_detail: first line medical therapy for a pituitary macroadenoma causing chiasmal compression
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar seeing a 34 year old woman referred by her general practitioner. Her periods stopped eight months ago and she has noticed a milky discharge from both breasts when she showers. Over the past two months she has twice walked into the left hand door frame of her kitchen.

She takes no regular medicines, has never taken an antipsychotic or metoclopramide, and a urinary pregnancy test in the clinic is negative. Formal perimetry shows loss in both upper outer quadrants. Her results and imaging are available at the consultation.

data_table.Examination: Bitemporal upper quadrant field loss on confrontation and on formal perimetry, visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally, no ophthalmoplegia
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 9800 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, free thyroxine within normal limits, creatinine within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Magnetic resonance imaging shows an 18 mm pituitary adenoma with suprasellar extension abutting and elevating the optic chiasm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Urgent transsphenoidal surgical decompression of the pituitary lesion
options.rationale: Surgery is the first line approach for most other pituitary macroadenomas causing chiasmal compression, which is exactly why this option is tempting, but the lactotroph tumour is the exception because it shrinks reliably on medical therapy. Surgery is reserved for dopamine agonist resistance, intolerance, or apoplexy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Oral cabergoline twice weekly with visual fields repeated at six weeks
options.rationale: A dopamine agonist normalises prolactin and shrinks tumour volume in the large majority of these adenomas, with field improvement often evident within weeks, so it is first line even when the chiasm is already compressed. Cabergoline is preferred over bromocriptine for efficacy and tolerability. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Stereotactic radiotherapy to the pituitary with endocrine follow up
options.rationale: Radiotherapy works slowly over years and carries a high rate of subsequent hypopituitarism, so it has no role as initial treatment when vision is threatened now. It is a third line option after both medical and surgical therapy have failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive alone with repeat imaging in six months
options.rationale: Replacing oestrogen treats the consequence of the hypogonadism but does nothing to the tumour, and leaving an adenoma that is already lifting the chiasm for six months risks permanent field loss. Oestrogen replacement is appropriate only once the tumour is controlled. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Observation with repeat prolactin and pituitary imaging in six months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is reasonable for a small intrasellar lesion with normal fields, not for a lesion that has already produced a bitemporal defect. The field loss is the indication to treat now. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: Prolactin secreting adenomas are the commonest functioning pituitary tumour and are unique among them in responding to medical therapy well enough that drugs displace surgery as first line, even for large lesions compressing the chiasm. Before accepting the diagnosis the treating doctor must exclude the common secondary causes of a raised prolactin, principally dopamine antagonist drugs, pregnancy, primary hypothyroidism and renal failure, because these produce modest elevations that do not need imaging. The height of the prolactin helps: levels above about 5000 mIU/L are almost always tumoural, whereas a mild rise alongside a large adenoma suggests stalk compression by a non lactotroph mass, a distinction that changes management entirely. Field defects typically improve within weeks of starting a dopamine agonist and perimetry is the practical early measure of response. Long term issues include the need to monitor for impulse control disorders on dopamine agonists and consideration of cardiac valve surveillance at higher cumulative doses.
key_points: Exclude drugs, pregnancy, hypothyroidism and renal failure before attributing a raised prolactin to a tumour
Levels above about 5000 mIU/L with a macroadenoma indicate a lactotroph tumour rather than stalk effect
A dopamine agonist is first line even with chiasmal compression, unlike other pituitary macroadenomas
Repeat perimetry at about six weeks is the practical early marker of response
Reserve surgery for resistance, intolerance or apoplexy
explanation.pearls: A prolactin of only 1000 to 2000 mIU/L alongside a large pituitary mass argues against a prolactinoma and for stalk compression by a non secreting tumour, which will not shrink on cabergoline and needs surgery instead.

subtopic_detail: acting on a frailty assessment rather than chronological age before major elective surgery
stem:
You are the registrar in the pre admission clinic assessing an 82 year old woman listed for elective open repair of a 6.1 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. The vascular surgeon has asked for a medical opinion on her fitness.

She lives alone in a unit and uses a four wheeled frame indoors. Her daughter does her shopping and manages her medicines in a dose administration aid, and she has stopped going to her weekly card group because she tires. She has lost 6 kg over the past year without trying. She tells you she wants to do whatever will let her stay in her own home. Her cardiac and respiratory examination is unremarkable and her recent bloods are unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Timed up and go test 22 seconds, grip strength reduced, no murmurs, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115 to 165), creatinine within normal limits, albumin 31 g/L (35 to 50), electrocardiogram sinus rhythm
data_table.Functional assessment: Clinical Frailty Scale score 6, requires assistance with shopping and medicines, independent with personal care

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed to surgery as listed since age alone does not preclude repair
options.rationale: The principle is correct but it is being applied to the wrong variable. The concern here is not her age but a Clinical Frailty Scale score of 6 with unintentional weight loss and a slow timed up and go, all of which independently predict postoperative mortality and loss of independence. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

options.text: Cancel the operation and refer to the palliative care service instead
options.rationale: A frailty score of 6 raises operative risk substantially but does not make repair futile, and a 6.1 cm aneurysm carries a real rupture risk if left. Withdrawing the surgical option outright forecloses a decision that has not yet been properly informed. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery

options.text: Refer for comprehensive geriatric assessment before the operation is listed
options.rationale: Structured multidimensional assessment with targeted optimisation of nutrition, function, medicines and cognition reduces postoperative complications and length of stay in frail surgical patients, and it generates the risk information she needs to weigh repair against her stated goal of remaining at home. It also frames the endovascular alternative properly. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

options.text: Arrange dobutamine stress echocardiography before making any decision
options.rationale: Functional cardiac testing is indicated when there are active cardiac symptoms or poor exercise tolerance of cardiac origin, neither of which is present. Ordering it here adds delay and answers a question that is not the one limiting her. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Start oral nutritional supplements and re-review in the clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: Addressing the low albumin and weight loss is a legitimate part of prehabilitation, but delivering it as an isolated intervention without assessing function, cognition, medicines and goals leaves most of the modifiable risk untouched. It is one component of the fuller assessment rather than a substitute for it. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

explanation.summary: Frailty is a state of reduced physiological reserve that predicts adverse surgical outcomes far better than age or than any single organ based risk score, and it is now routinely assessed before major elective surgery in Australian practice. The Clinical Frailty Scale grades from 1 for very fit to 9 for terminally ill, with 5 and above denoting increasing degrees of frailty and 6 indicating dependence for all outside activities and some personal care. Comprehensive geriatric assessment examines medical, functional, cognitive, nutritional, medication and social domains together and pairs the findings with a targeted intervention plan, and randomised evidence in older surgical and orthopaedic populations shows reductions in delirium, complications and length of stay. The assessment also surfaces what matters to the patient, which is decisive when the choice is between an intervention that prevents a future rupture and one that preserves current independence. For aortic disease specifically, the assessment output often reframes the discussion toward an endovascular approach with a shorter recovery.
key_points: Frailty predicts postoperative outcome better than chronological age
Clinical Frailty Scale 5 and above signals frailty, with 6 indicating dependence for outside activities
Comprehensive geriatric assessment reduces delirium, complications and length of stay in frail surgical patients
Unintentional weight loss, slow gait speed and weak grip are individually prognostic
Assessment output should be tied to the patient's own stated goals
explanation.pearls: A timed up and go of more than 15 seconds before major elective surgery predicts a markedly increased rate of postoperative complications and one year mortality, and is a two minute bedside test that outperforms most preoperative bloods.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine
Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery
Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand
